Nobody bought a Halloween costume at our house. A week before, Mom dragged out the rag bag and told you to get creative. You ended up a hobo with a burnt-cork beard, or a ghost in an old bedsheet with the eyeholes cut a little crooked. Then she handed you a pillowcase, the big one, and said be back by eight. You walked every street in the neighborhood until your feet hurt and that pillowcase weighed more than your little brother. Dumping it out on the living room rug was the best part of the whole year.
column6:
I went as a ghost three years running because my mother had one sheet she was willing to sacrifice. By the third year the eyeholes had stretched so wide you could see my whole face. Nobody on our street cared, they just handed over the popcorn balls.

column2: Every family vacation started with Dad spreading the road map across the steering wheel at the first gas stop. He'd trace the route with his finger like a general planning an invasion. Mom held it on her lap the rest of the way, calling out turns a little too late. Somewhere around the state line, somebody tried to fold it back up. It never went back the same way. By the end of the trip that map was a lump of creases the size of a sofa cushion, and it lived in the glove box for the next ten years.
column6:
My father would not stop to ask directions if the car was on fire. My mother would quietly hand him the map, upside down, just to make a point. We always got there, usually about an hour after we should have.

column2: You knew you were in trouble when Mom stopped yelling. She'd go real quiet, look at the kitchen clock, and say the words. Wait till your father gets home. Then she went right back to peeling potatoes like nothing happened. You sat at that table and listened to every car that went by. Every one of them sounded like his. By the time Dad finally walked in, you'd already served about four hours of your sentence, and half the time he was too tired to add to it.
column6:
My mother used that line maybe five times my whole childhood, and she only needed to. I remember listening for the sound of my dad's tires on the gravel driveway like it was the end of the world. He usually just sighed and asked what's for supper.

column2: A handshake used to settle it. If a man said he'd be there Saturday morning, he was there Saturday morning.
column6:
My grandfather sold a tractor to a neighbor on a handshake and got paid in installments over two years. Never a paper signed, never a payment late. He said a man's word was the only thing he owned that nobody could take from him.

column2: The room sounded like a hailstorm on a tin roof. Forty manual typewriters, all going at once, and every few seconds somebody's bell went ding and the carriage slammed back. The teacher walked the rows with a stopwatch and a ruler, and if she caught you peeking at the keys, she'd drape a sheet of paper right over your hands. You typed the same drill until your fingers knew it in their sleep. Nobody thought much of it at the time. Funny how that's the class most of us ended up using every single day.
column6:
I took typing my sophomore year because a friend said it was an easy grade. It was not. But I can still type without looking, and I owe every bit of that to a woman with cat-eye glasses and absolutely no mercy.

column2: Every house had one, and it was never in a sewing box. It was in a round blue cookie tin that hadn't held a cookie since Eisenhower. If you lost a button, you didn't buy one, you went digging. On a rainy day Mom would dump the whole thing out on the kitchen table and let you sort them by color. Brass ones off Dad's old Navy coat, little pearl ones off a christening gown, a wooden toggle nobody could place. You could spend an entire afternoon in there and never get bored.
column6:
I still have my grandmother's button tin on a shelf in my sewing room. Every once in a while I open it just to hear that sound when you run your hand through them. There's a red glass one in there I've never matched to anything, and I never will.

column2: You didn't carry a phone, you carried a dime. Mom made sure there was one in your pocket every time you left the house, just in case. The booth sat on the corner by the drugstore, glass on three sides and a folding door that squeaked. The phone book hung on a chain and half the pages were torn out. It didn't matter. You knew every number that mattered by heart, and you could dial home in the dark.
column6:
I can still tell you the phone number of the house I grew up in, and my best friend's, and my grandmother's. I can't tell you my own cell number without looking at it. Some things the brain just decides to keep.

column2: One bathroom. Six people. A water heater that gave out after the second shower. You learned to get up early.
column6:
I was the youngest, so I got the cold water every single morning until I was fourteen. I finally started setting my alarm for 5:30 just to beat my sisters. I've been an early riser ever since, and I blame that water heater.

column2: Sunday afternoon, after the last car pulled out, Dad drove us over to the empty church lot and switched seats. He gave you one speech about the clutch and then never said another calm word. The car bucked like a mule. It stalled. It rolled backward toward the rectory. Dad gripped the dashboard and stared straight ahead with his jaw set. And somewhere around the fortieth try, it caught, and you drove a slow, perfect circle while he finally let out his breath.
column6:
Our car was a three-on-the-tree Ford that had been through two owners before us. My father said exactly four things that afternoon and three of them I can't repeat in church. But I drove us home, and he let me.

column2: In a small town, you didn't dial the number, you picked up the receiver and told her who you wanted. She'd plug the cord into the right hole and put you through. She knew which line was the doctor and which was the feed store. She knew who was calling the girl on Elm Street every night at seven. She never said a word about any of it, at least not on the job. Every town had one, and every town was a little safer because she was listening.
column6:
My great-aunt worked the switchboard in a town of about nine hundred people. She said she could tell who was calling just by the way they said hello. She took most of what she heard to her grave, and she was proud of that.
